subsection: 5. Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration

notes.h: Key terms: ethnic group, race and religion
notes.b: When people move, they carry their culture, appearance and beliefs with them. These three categories overlap but are not the same, and migration can bring all three into contact in one place.
points: An ethnic group is a group of people who share culture, language, ancestry, traditions or religion, which is why members often feel they belong to the same community.
A race is a group classed by physical traits such as skin colour. Race is a social idea with no biological basis for ranking people, so no race is naturally better than another.
Religion is a shared system of belief and practice. It can cut across ethnic and racial groups, so people of different ethnic groups or races may share one religion.
A multi-ethnic society contains several ethnic groups living together. A multicultural society goes further: it is one in which those groups keep distinct cultural practices.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how ethnic and religious issues arise from migration, so be able to define ethnic group, race and religion in a line each and keep them apart.

notes.b: When migrants and the host population meet, the result can be hostility or acceptance. These terms name the attitudes, the settlement patterns and the policies that governments use in response.
points: Racism is prejudice (an unfair opinion formed in advance) or discrimination (unfair treatment) based on race or ethnicity.
Xenophobia is fear or hostility towards foreigners. Islamophobia is prejudice against Muslims, so it targets people because of their religion.

Segregation is the clustering of migrants in particular areas. It happens either by choice, for support, cheap housing and chain migration (earlier migrants helping relatives and neighbours to follow them), or because discrimination forces migrants there.
Assimilation is the adoption of the majority culture by migrants, so their own culture is gradually given up.
Integration is the joining of migrants to society while they keep some of their own culture.
Multiculturalism is the acceptance of several cultures as equal within one society, so no single culture is treated as the norm.
notes.tip: Government approach is part of every case study answer, so know the difference between assimilation, integration and multiculturalism and say which one each country follows.

notes.h: How ethnic, racial and religious issues arise
notes.b: Tensions rarely come from difference alone. They arise from circumstances, discrimination and politics, and the same general mechanisms appear in each of the case studies below.
points: Competition for jobs, housing and services, especially in recessions (periods when the economy shrinks and jobs are scarce), and fear that migrants will undercut wages by working for less.
Visible difference, such as skin colour or dress like the hijab (the headscarf worn by some Muslim women), makes minorities easy targets of prejudice.

Religious practice in public space can clash with secular (non-religious) or majority-religion norms. Examples are places of worship, dress, halal food (food prepared according to Islamic rules), holy days and faith schools.
Residential segregation and concentration in deprived areas reinforce poverty and separation, because people who live apart have fewer chances to mix at school or work.
Language barriers in schools, work and services make it harder for migrants to take part fully.
Political exploitation: far-right and anti-immigration parties and movements, and misinformation on social media, turn worries into hostility.
Second-generation issues: children born in the host country may face discrimination and conflict over identity, since they belong to two cultures.
Positive outcomes include cultural enrichment through food, music, sport and festivals, new places of worship, intercultural schools and mixed marriages.
notes.tip: A 30-mark Higher answer on how these issues arise needs mechanisms such as jobs, housing, visible difference, religious practice, segregation and the far right, illustrated by Ireland and France, with government policy. Present tensions as arising from circumstances, discrimination and politics, and avoid stereotypes.

notes.h: Case study: Ireland's growing diversity and religious change
notes.b: Ireland moved from a mostly white, Catholic society to a diverse one from the 1990s. The census shows both the new nationalities and the shift in religion.
points: Census 2022: about one in five people (just over 1 million) were born outside Ireland, and about 630,000 were non-Irish nationals (about 12%).
The largest non-Irish groups are Polish, UK, Indian, Romanian, Lithuanian and Brazilian.
Census 2022: about 69% of people were Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in 2016, so the majority religion is shrinking in share.
Census 2022: about 14% had no religion, up from about 10% in 2016.
Census 2022 counted about 82,000 Muslims, about 100,000 Orthodox Christians and about 33,000 Hindus, showing growth in religions that were once rare in Ireland.
The Islamic Cultural Centre of Ireland is in Clonskeagh, Dublin, an example of a new place of worship and community centre.
About 9 in 10 primary schools are under Catholic patronage (the Catholic Church runs them), so religion once decided many school admissions.
notes.tip: Use Ireland as a main case study. Give the change from a mostly white, Catholic society, the religious change, and the school admissions issue, and describe residential concentration without naming Irish suburbs.

notes.b: Rapid change brought hostility as well as welcome. Several incidents show how housing pressure and anti-immigration feeling can turn to protest and violence.
points: East Wall, Dublin: protests from November 2022 against housing international protection applicants (people seeking asylum) in a former office building.
Dublin riot, 23 November 2023: after a knife attack on children outside a school on Parnell Square, buses, a Luas tram (Dublin's light-rail line) and shops were burned and looted.
Arson attacks (deliberate fires) on several buildings proposed for asylum accommodation (2023 to 2024).
Racism and hate crime (crime motivated by hatred of a group) accompany these tensions, and the protests show how hostility can turn to violence.
notes.tip: For the Dublin riot, give the trigger as a knife attack on children and the damage done. Do not name the attacker's nationality, speculate about motive or name the victims.

notes.b: Irish policy combines equality law, an integration strategy and anti-racism measures, with specific reforms to schools and recognition of Travellers. Each tackles an issue raised in the earlier blocks.
points: The Employment Equality Act 1998 and the Equal Status Act 2000 prohibit discrimination on nine grounds, including race, religion and membership of the Traveller community.
The Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 is an earlier law against hatred, so Ireland had some protection before the recent migration.
The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission was established in 2014 to promote and protect human rights and equality.
The Migrant Integration Strategy ran from 2017 to 2020, aiming to help migrants join Irish society.
The National Action Plan Against Racism was published in March 2023.
The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 gives tougher sentences for crimes motivated by hatred of a protected characteristic (such as race or religion).

The Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 removed the baptism barrier, so most Catholic primary schools can no longer use religion to decide admissions. Educate Together, a multi-denominational school body founded in 1984, runs schools open to all faiths and none.
Irish Travellers were formally recognised by the State as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.
notes.tip: Always pair issues with policy responses. Name the laws with their years, the school admission reform and Educate Together, and the recognition of Traveller ethnicity.

notes.h: Ireland: evaluation and the Traveller community
notes.b: Judging Irish policy means asking whether the laws have worked in practice. The Traveller community also belongs in this discussion, but not as migrants.
points: The legal framework is strong, but the 2022 to 2023 protests show that hostility persists.

Direct provision (the system of housing asylum applicants in centres while their claims are processed) isolates applicants in rural centres, and this works against integration. There is more on this in Migration policy in Ireland and the EU.
The Traveller community is an indigenous Irish ethnic minority, not a migrant group, so it is included here only as part of Irish ethnic policy.
About 33,000 Travellers were counted in Census 2022.
notes.tip: Say clearly that Travellers are an indigenous Irish ethnic minority and not migrants, and include them only as part of Irish ethnic policy.

notes.h: Case study: France, North African migration and laïcité
notes.b: France has a large Muslim population and a strict model of secularism, and it follows an assimilation approach. Its laws on religious dress show how the model works in practice.
points: Post-war immigrant labour came from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Portugal. Large-scale Algerian migration followed the Algerian War of Independence (1954 to 1962) and Algeria's independence in 1962.
France has the largest Muslim population in western Europe.
Laïcité, the principle of strict separation of religion and state, dates from the 1905 law. This is why the state treats religion as a private matter.
A 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, in state schools.
A 2010 law banned face coverings, such as the burqa and niqab (veils covering the face), in public places, in force from 2011.
Banlieues are segregated high-rise estates on the edge of cities, with high unemployment, so residents are concentrated in deprived areas apart from the city centre.
notes.tip: Do not swap the dates: laïcité dates from the 1905 law, the headscarf law is 2004 and applies to schools, and the face-covering ban is 2010 and applies to public places. France follows assimilation, so everyone is a French citizen and there are no official ethnic statistics.

notes.h: Case study: France, unrest, attacks and the far right
notes.b: In the banlieues, segregation and unemployment have fed unrest. Terrorist attacks and politics have then added to tension with the Muslim community.
points: The October to November 2005 riots began in Clichy-sous-Bois, a Paris banlieue, after two teenagers died fleeing police. They spread across France and a state of emergency (special powers for the government) was declared.
June 2023 riots followed the police shooting of a 17-year-old in Nanterre.
The Charlie Hebdo attack in January 2015 and the Paris attacks of 13 November 2015 (130 killed) were followed by rising Islamophobia.
The National Front, a far-right party founded in 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, was renamed the National Rally (Rassemblement National) in 2018 under Marine Le Pen.
notes.tip: Use France as a main case study alongside Ireland. Name the banlieue Clichy-sous-Bois for the 2005 riots, and link the issues to the assimilation approach and the far right.

notes.h: Case study: Germany and Turkish guest workers
notes.b: Germany recruited workers to rebuild its economy, expecting them to leave. Many stayed, and the question of their citizenship shaped integration for decades.
points: A recruitment agreement with Turkey was signed in 1961, and recruitment of guest workers (Gastarbeiter, workers invited for a limited time) stopped in 1973.
Guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and brought their families.
Germany long denied them citizenship, and segregated districts formed, such as Kreuzberg in Berlin, which has a large Turkish community.
The 2000 citizenship law gave citizenship to children born in Germany to long-resident foreign parents.
The 2024 reform allowed dual citizenship (holding two nationalities) generally and shortened the residence requirement.
About 3 million people of Turkish origin live in Germany (2020s).
The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), founded in 2013, grew after the 2015 refugee arrivals on an anti-immigration platform, so it is an example of political exploitation of migration.
notes.tip: Kreuzberg in Berlin is the segregated district to name for Germany.

notes.h: Case study: Britain and the Windrush generation
notes.b: Caribbean migrants arrived in Britain from 1948. Their arrival shows racism in housing and work, and how policy later had to respond.
points: The Empire Windrush, a ship, arrived at Tilbury (a port on the Thames) in June 1948 with passengers from the Caribbean.
Caribbean migrants faced racism in housing and work, which made it harder for them to settle, for example in finding a home to rent or a job.
The Notting Hill riots in London in 1958 showed racial tension turning violent.
The Race Relations Act 1965 was the first UK law against racial discrimination.
The Windrush scandal of 2018: long-settled Caribbean-born residents were wrongly detained, denied services or deported because they lacked documents.

notes.h: Case study: Northern Ireland and the Plantation of Ulster
notes.b: The Plantation was a historic migration whose religious legacy still divides Northern Ireland. Here it is studied only as a migration and its religious legacy.
points: The Plantation of Ulster began in 1609, after the Flight of the Earls (1607). Land taken from Catholic Irish was settled by Protestant colonists from Scotland and England.
Centuries of religious and political division followed, leading to the Troubles (the conflict) from the late 1960s to 1998, in which about 3,500 people were killed.
The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998.
Census 2021 (Northern Ireland): about 46% Catholic and about 43% Protestant and other Christian.
Most children attend schools of their own community, and peace walls (barriers) still divide some Belfast neighbourhoods, so the division is still visible in housing and schooling.
notes.tip: Keep this to the Plantation as a migration and its religious legacy. Partition, nationalism and the full conflict belong to another topic.

notes.b: The Roma are an example of an ethnic minority that has been on the move for centuries and has often been excluded wherever it settles.
points: The Roma are about 10 to 12 million people in Europe (Council of Europe estimate) and Europe's largest ethnic minority.
The Roma originated in northern India and migrated to Europe about 1,000 years ago.
The Roma have faced discrimination in housing, education and employment, and segregated schooling in parts of central and eastern Europe.
France expelled Roma to Romania and Bulgaria in 2010, which drew EU criticism, so exclusion has come from governments as well as individuals.

notes.b: The case studies show three different responses to migrant minorities. Comparing them is a good way to finish an answer on government policy.
points: France's assimilation model treats all citizens alike and collects no official ethnic statistics.
Ireland's approach rests on equality law and an integration strategy.
Germany moved from excluding guest workers from citizenship to citizenship reform in 2000 and 2024.
notes.tip: Pair each country's issues with its policy response, since examiners expect government policy in the answer.

questions.prompt: Examine how ethnic and religious issues can arise as a result of migration.
questions.model: Issues arise through competition for jobs, housing and services, visible difference, religious practice in public space, residential segregation, language barriers, political exploitation and second-generation identity conflict. In France, laïcité shapes the response: the 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the headscarf, in state schools, and the 2010 law banned face coverings in public places. Segregated banlieues of high-rise estates, with high unemployment, were the setting for the October to November 2005 riots, which began in Clichy-sous-Bois, and for the June 2023 riots. Terrorist attacks in 2015 were followed by rising Islamophobia, and the National Rally has exploited anti-immigration feeling. In Ireland, religious change has been rapid: Census 2022 showed about 69% Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in 2016, with about 14% of people having no religion. Most primary schools are under Catholic patronage, so religion decided many admissions until the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 removed the baptism barrier. Racism and hate crime appeared in the East Wall protests from November 2022 and the Dublin riot of 23 November 2023, which followed a knife attack on children outside a school and in which buses, a Luas tram and shops were burned and looted. Government responses include the Employment Equality Act 1998, the Equal Status Act 2000, the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (2014), the Migrant Integration Strategy, the National Action Plan Against Racism (2023) and the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024. Evaluation: issues arise from circumstances, discrimination and politics rather than from migrants themselves, and the reforms show that policy can reduce them, although the protests show that hostility persists.

questions.prompt: Describe and evaluate government policy in Ireland on ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
questions.model: Ireland's equality law covers discrimination on nine grounds, including race, religion and membership of the Traveller community, under the Employment Equality Act 1998 and the Equal Status Act 2000, and the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 is an earlier safeguard. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission was established in 2014 to enforce these protections. The Migrant Integration Strategy ran from 2017 to 2020, and the National Action Plan Against Racism was published in March 2023. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 gives tougher sentences for crimes motivated by hatred of a protected characteristic. School policy changed through the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018, which removed the baptism barrier, and through Educate Together, founded in 1984 as a multi-denominational body. Irish Travellers were recognised as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017. Evaluation: the legal framework is comprehensive, and school admissions reform addresses one long-standing barrier. However, the East Wall protests from November 2022 and the Dublin riot of 23 November 2023 show that hostility persists, and direct provision, which isolates asylum applicants in rural centres, works against integration. Policy has been strongest on law and schools and weakest where housing and community pressures meet migration.

questions.prompt: Migration can lead to racial and religious tension. Discuss with reference to one European country other than Ireland.
questions.model: Germany is the example. A recruitment agreement with Turkey signed in 1961 brought guest workers (Gastarbeiter), who were recruited until 1973. Guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and brought families, so the Turkish community became established, with Kreuzberg in Berlin a district where it is large. Germany long denied these long-term residents citizenship, which fed segregation and tension. The 2000 citizenship law gave citizenship to children born in Germany to long-resident foreign parents, and the 2024 reform allowed dual citizenship generally and shortened the residence requirement. About 3 million people of Turkish origin live in Germany. Racial and religious tensions were sharpened by the 2015 refugee arrivals, when Germany received the largest number of asylum seekers in the EU, and by the rise of the Alternative für Deutschland, founded in 2013, which grew after 2015 on an anti-immigration platform. Evaluation: tensions arose because of exclusion, segregation and political exploitation rather than because of migration alone, and the citizenship reforms show that policy can reduce them.
